title: Graphs, DFS, and BFS
summary: Model connections as nodes and edges, then explore them with a stack or a queue.
keyPoints: A graph is a set of nodes and edges; it can have cycles, unlike a tree.
Adjacency lists use O(V + E) space and are the usual interview representation.
DFS follows one branch deeply; BFS explores in rings of distance.
A visited set is what prevents infinite loops in a cyclic graph.
A grid is a graph where each cell connects to its four neighbors.

complexity.note: The list stores each edge once or twice.

commonMistakes: Forgetting the visited set, which causes infinite loops on cycles.
Marking a node visited when it is popped instead of when it is enqueued, which adds duplicates.
Using DFS when the problem asks for the shortest number of steps; BFS is required for unweighted shortest paths.
Treating a grid boundary check as optional and indexing outside the array.
interviewNotes: Ask whether the graph is directed, weighted, connected, or may contain cycles.
Say what the queue or stack contains and what invariant it maintains.
For a grid, describe the four (or eight) neighbor directions explicitly.

checkYourself.question: Why does BFS find the shortest path in an unweighted graph?
checkYourself.answer: It visits all nodes at distance d before any node at distance d + 1, so the first visit to a node is through a shortest path.

checkYourself.question: How much space does an adjacency list use?
checkYourself.answer: O(V + E), because it stores one list per node and one entry per edge.

checkYourself.question: How do you count connected components?
checkYourself.answer: Loop over every node. When you find an unvisited node, run DFS or BFS to mark its whole component and increment the count.
